summary: A 1970 proposed user-user protocol by G. H. Mealy.

eli5.summary: A proposal for rules letting people on different computers talk to each other.

questions: what is a logical record in the arpanet
subtitle: A 1970 proposal for a layer above the Host-Host protocol that lets programs exchange records, control data and status.

tldr.problem: The IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST protocols do not let two user programs agree on data formats, and they do not check that a requested action was actually carried out by the other side.
tldr.mechanism: George Mealy proposes a USER-USER protocol in which every segment of data is preceded by a 4-bit OPERATION flag, and often a COUNT, that says what the data is and how long it is.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a proposal and a sketch of one PDP-10 implementation at Harvard, not a finished standard. It leaves login and interrupt handling as open questions.

today: The metadata gives this RFC an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a 1970 proposal, and the text itself calls it a starting point rather than a settled protocol.

sections.title: Why a User-User Protocol
sections.content:
Mealy argues that, for a user program, talking over the Network should look like ordinary input/output. At Harvard, each link would be treated as a logical device on the PDP-10, so that existing programs could use the Network without modification, at least with other PDP-10s.

That only goes so far. The IBM 360 has logical devices but the PDP-10 does not. With no Network standard for integers or reals (which he says he would oppose), two processes must agree locally on data conversion. Finally, the IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST protocols do not check that a requested action was really done, so he leaves that to the USER-USER level.

He judges any proposal by three criteria: the notion of a logical record should be present and message suppressed; existing programs should be able to reach files anywhere in the Network unchanged; and the protocol should be implementable in any HOST at the SVC or UUO level.
sections.eli5: Different computers store things in different ways. The author wants a small set of tags so two programs can agree how to talk, and can check that the other side really did what was asked.

sections.title: Flags, Counts and Data Blocks
sections.content:
The protocol applies to the data bits in a message, between the marking bits and the padding bits. The IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST protocols are unaffected. Everything on a link is a sequence of flags followed by possibly empty data blocks, in the form OPERATION, COUNT, DATA.

The OPERATION field is always present and is four bits long. The COUNT field, when present, gives the number of data bytes that follow, and is 8 bits long (16 bits in the EOM flag). The byte size comes from the last SIZE flag, and a SIZE flag must appear in each message before any block flag except ASCII.

EOM restates the total bit count of the message as an error check and must appear at the end of each message unless ESC has appeared. The separators RS, GS and FS mark the end of a record, group and file; a record need not fit inside one message. CONTROL means roughly 'try to do the following' and STATUS reports back, with meanings left to local agreement. SYS would let a program talk to a foreign HOST directly, for example for logging on.
sections.eli5: Each piece of data gets a tag first. Some tags say 'here come this many bytes', and some just say 'end of line' or 'end of file'.

sections.title: The PDP-10 Implementation Sketch
sections.content:
Mealy sketches Harvard's plan as five UUOs: PUTF (put flag), PUTD (put data), PUT (put record), GETFD (get flag or data) and GET (get record). The first version would be user routines, with the monitor version used for description.

A file transfer is shown as a flag sequence. To fetch a file, the requester sends CONTROL data with OPEN parameters and a LABEL for the lookup, then EOM to force transmission. The server answers with STATUS, SIZE and LABEL, and each record is requested with a CONTROL flag and answered with STATUS and a logical record, ending with a CLOSE request.

He estimates the PDP-10 space needed at about 400 instructions, split equally between input and output. He leaves LOGON handling and interrupt-on-link as open questions, and suggests SYS might replace dedicated sockets for logon.
sections.eli5: The author shows how his own computer would send and receive these tagged pieces, like a recipe for fetching a file one chunk at a time.

items.label: NUL
items.desc: No operation; consider the next flag.

items.label: ESC
items.desc: Escape to local convention for flags.

items.label: EOM N
items.desc: End of message; N is the total bit count.

items.label: SYS N
items.desc: N bytes of data for the receiving HOST system.

items.label: CONTROL N
items.desc: N bytes of control data follow.

items.label: STATUS N
items.desc: N bytes of status data follow.

items.label: LABEL N
items.desc: N bytes of identification data follow.

items.label: KEY N
items.desc: N bytes of key data follow.

items.label: ASCII N
items.desc: N (8-bit) bytes of ASCII data follow.
